sub.en: Look at the phrases. Which agree, which disagree — and which do both at once?

items.q: “___ my opinion, privacy is not dead.”
“I’m afraid I ___.”
items.why: “I’m afraid I disagree” is the standard polite disagreement. The “I’m afraid” is what makes it polite.

items.q: “I ___ your point, but I’m not sure about that.”
items.why: “I take your point, but…” agrees first and disagrees second. It is the most useful phrase in the lesson.

tts: Excuse me, can I ask you a question? — Well, OK, but I’m late for work, so if you’re quick.
Some media experts are saying privacy is dead in our twenty-first century world. Do you agree? — No, I’m afraid I disagree, although you do see a lot more cameras around. I mean the CCTV ones.

And what do you think about that? — Well, it’s important to feel safe these days, isn’t it? So I don’t mind them. I take your point that somebody is watching, but I would rather be watched than robbed.

acts.title: Two minutes on: should phones be banned in schools?
text: Good morning. My name’s Aigul and I’m going to talk for two minutes about whether phones should be banned in schools. I’ll give you the case for, the case against, and then what I actually think.

FIRSTLY, the case for banning them. The research is fairly clear: in schools that removed phones, test results went up, and they went up most for the students who were doing worst. That is not nothing.
IN ADDITION, teachers report fewer arguments and more talking in the corridors. One head teacher said the school “sounded different” within a month.

ON THE OTHER HAND, a ban is easy to announce and hard to run. Somebody has to collect four hundred phones every morning and give them back, and if a parent needs to reach a child during the day, the school becomes the only route.

IN MY OPINION, the honest answer is that it works and that it costs something. I’d ban them in lessons, not in the building. I take the point that a half-measure is harder to enforce, but a rule nobody enforces is worse than a smaller rule that everybody does.
TO SUM UP: it works, it isn’t free, and I would still do it. Thanks for listening. Any questions?

write.q: Write a two-minute presentation on a question you have an opinion about: 10–12 lines. Follow the model’s six moves, and use Firstly, In addition, On the other hand, In my opinion and To sum up. Give the other side fairly before you give your own view.
write.model: Good morning. My name’s Marat and I’m going to talk for two minutes about whether the working week should be four days. I’ll give the case for, the case against, and what I think. FIRSTLY, the trials are surprisingly consistent: in most of them output stayed the same and people took fewer sick days. IN ADDITION, the companies that tried it found it easier to hire. ON THE OTHER HAND, it works best in offices, and most people here do not work in offices — you cannot run a hospital or a bakery four days a week. IN MY OPINION, the honest version is that this is a change for some jobs and not for others, and pretending otherwise is why people stop listening. I’d start with the jobs where it clearly works and measure it for two years. I take the point that this creates two classes of worker. TO SUM UP: it works, it doesn’t work everywhere, and we should say so. Thanks for listening. Any questions?

speak.q: Give your two-minute presentation out loud, using all five signposts. Then respond to these two opinions: “Phones should be banned completely” and “Nobody reads any more.” Agree with one and half-agree with the other.
speak.model: Firstly… In addition… On the other hand… In my opinion… To sum up. — I’m afraid I disagree about banning them completely; a rule nobody enforces is worse than a smaller one. — I take your point about reading, but people read all day now. It just isn’t books.
